title: Wood Provision
text:
This site documents, step by step and in R, the update of the wood provision ecosystem service for the European Union. Wood provision is the contribution of forest ecosystems to the growth of trees that can be used as timber. The work follows the accounting approach of the EU Knowledge Innovation Project on an Integrated system of Natural Capital and ecosystem services Accounting (INCA).
Each page is a runnable document, so the procedure can be inspected and repeated from the repository.

Wood provision builds the physical accounts. It estimates the net annual increment of forest available for wood supply by country for 2000 to 2024, compares it with removals to flag overuse, and maps it at 1 km and 100 m resolution over the forest of each year, weighted by the productivity of the vegetation.
Monetary valuation gives that flow a value in euro, in current and constant (2010) prices, and maps it.

The tables and maps produced are available for download at the end of each page. The 100 m maps are too large for the repository and are kept in an external folder.

title: Wood Provision: Monetary Valuation
text:
This page continues the wood provision update. The physical accounts produced the net annual increment (NAI) of forest available for wood supply (FAWS) by country and year, and mapped it. This page gives that flow a monetary value, expresses it in constant prices and maps it.
The method is the one of INCA Part III (La Notte et al., 2021) as implemented in the INCA plugin, so that results are comparable with it. It needs three Eurostat inputs and one deflator.

Value of standing timber. for_sup_cp reports the output of forest trees (P1_TR) in million euro (Eurostat, 2026c). Dividing it by NAI gives a unit value in euro per cubic metre. It is reported by few countries in the early years.
Unit value of roundwood exports. for_basic reports export value and volume of roundwood (Eurostat, 2026b). It is reported by almost every country and year.
Ratio between the two. Where both unit values exist, their ratio links the well-covered export price to the sparse timber price. The ratio is completed with averages and applied backwards: unit value of NAI = export unit value / ratio.
Deflator. The EU27 Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) converts nominal values to constant prices (Eurostat, 2026a).

The physical flow is not recomputed here. The page reads the tables that the physical accounts exported to data/outputs/results/, so both documents stay consistent.









Term
Meaning in this document




Monetary value of the service
The value of the wood that the forest grows in a year, which is the net annual increment (NAI) times a price per cubic metre.


Unit value
A value divided by a volume, here euro per cubic metre.


Standing timber
Trees as they stand in the forest, before harvest. Its value is what the wood is worth before the costs of felling and transport.


Output of forest trees (P1_TR)
The item of the Eurostat forestry accounts that records the value of standing timber produced in a year.


Roundwood
Felled and cut timber, not yet processed. Its export price includes harvesting and transport, so it is higher than the value of standing timber.


Current prices
Values in the money of the year in which they occurred. Inflation makes them hard to compare across years.


Constant prices
Values converted to the prices of one base year, so that changes over time reflect quantities and not inflation.


Deflator
The factor that converts a current value to constant prices. It is the price index of the base year divided by the index of the year of the value.


HICP
The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices of Eurostat, used here as the general price index.






The value of standing timber is the ideal price for the service, but countries rarely report it, mainly before 2012. Roundwood export prices are reported by almost every country and year, but they include the costs of harvesting and transport, so they are not the same thing. The method uses the countries and years where both prices exist to measure how far apart the two are (the ratio). It then turns the well-covered export price into an estimate of the timber price by dividing by that ratio. In the years and countries with no timber price, the ratio is replaced by an average, which is the weakest part of the method and is reported openly in the tables below.






ImportantRun the physical document first



This page reads data/outputs/results/wood_nai_faws_country_year.rds and the 1 km weights in data/inputs/weights/. Both are committed to the repository, so nothing needs to be rerun unless the physical series changes.








NoteConstant prices use a single base year



The base year is base_year in the parameters chunk. It is set to 2010 so that this service shares one price level with the other ecosystem service accounts and can be added to or compared with them (the INCA plugin uses 2000). The choice of base year changes the level of the constant-price series but not its shape. Changing it does not touch the nominal values, because the deflator is applied in one step at the end.

title: Wood Provision: Monetary Valuation
text:
Parameters
A country with some observations is completed with its own average, because its price level is the best guide to its missing years. A country with no observations at all is completed with the EU average, taken over recent years, where coverage is better. The averages that complete the gaps use the same windows as the INCA plugin: the country mean over the whole series, and the EU mean over the more recent years. The plugin stops at 2021 because of the data it had; the window here runs to 2023, the last year with broad coverage.

years_all <- 2000:2024
years_report <- c(2000, 2006, 2012, 2018, 2024)
base_year <- 2010

# Windows for the averages that fill gaps
country_years <- 2000:2023
eu_years <- 2012:2023

# Inputs
nai_file <- "data/outputs/results/wood_nai_faws_country_year.rds"
overuse_file <- "data/outputs/results/wood_overuse_country_year.rds"
nuts_weights_file <- "data/inputs/weights/weight_by_nuts.rds"
sup_file <- "data/inputs/eurostat/for_sup_cp_p1tr.rds"
basic_file <- "data/inputs/eurostat/for_basic_rw_exports.rds"
hicp_file <- "data/inputs/eurostat/hicp_eu27.rds"
countries_file <- "data/inputs/gis/NUTS_RG_01M_2024_3035_LEVL0.gpkg"
weights_dir <- "data/inputs/weights"

# Outputs
results_dir <- "data/outputs/results"
gis_dir <- "data/outputs/gis"
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(gis_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

text:
Maps
The maps are shown at 10 km, as the sum of 100 cells of 1 km. The maps at 100 m are written by scripts/07_write_maps_100m.R, which applies the same key and checks that the cells of each country add up to its national value. They are too large for the repository and are in the external folder listed in the downloads.

map_data <- aggregate(value_maps, fact = 10, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("value_constant_"), names_to = "year", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(year = sub("value_constant_", "", year)) |>
  filter(value > 0)

ggplot(map_data) +
  geom_tile(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value)) +
  geom_sf(data = countries, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(transform = "sqrt", name = "Million euro\n(base-year prices)\nper 10 km cell") +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(2.6e6, 6.6e6), ylim = c(1.4e6, 5.4e6), datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: Wood Provision Ecosystem Service
text:
This page documents the R routine that updates the wood provision ecosystem service for the European Union and makes it spatially explicit. Wood provision is the ecosystem contribution to the growth of trees, and it is measured here with the net annual increment (NAI) of the forest available for wood supply (FAWS), in thousand cubic metres over bark (Eurostat, 2026a; La Notte et al., 2021). Each step is written so that users can read it, rerun it from the repository alone and reuse the parts that generalise.
The routine has five components, in this order:

the statistical component, which builds a complete country-by-year NAI series from Eurostat for_vol_efa (Eurostat, 2026b) for 2000 to 2024, and reports the years 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018 and 2024;
the overuse check, which compares removals with NAI and flags country-years in which removals exceed NAI;
the spatial component, which spreads each national NAI over the forest of the year, weighted by the productivity of the vegetation, so that the pixels of a country add up to its national value;
the exports, which write the tables and maps to data/outputs/ for download.



The terms below are used throughout the page.







Term
Meaning in this document




Ecosystem service
A contribution of ecosystems to human activity. Here it is the growth of trees that can be harvested as timber.


Net annual increment (NAI)
The average annual volume growth of living trees, minus the volume of trees that die naturally. It is the quantity of new wood the forest adds in a year, and it is the accounting measure of the service.


Over bark
Volumes include the bark of the tree, as in the Eurostat questionnaire.


Thousand m3
The unit of the volumes (1,000 cubic metres), as reported by Eurostat.


Forest available for wood supply (FAWS)
Forest where no environmental, social or economic restriction significantly limits wood supply. Protected areas, steep slopes or remote forests are typical restrictions.


Forest not available for wood supply (FNAWS)
Forest with such restrictions.


Corine Land Cover (CLC) accounting layers
European land cover maps at 100 m for 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018 and 2024. Forest is taken from them.


Gross Dry Matter Productivity (GDMP)
The rate at which vegetation produces dry matter, in kilograms per hectare and day, estimated from satellite images every ten days.


Removals
The volume of wood actually taken out of the forest in a year, which is close to the volume harvested.


Overuse
Removals greater than NAI. Harvesting more than the forest grows depletes the stock of timber, so the service is not sustained.


Spatial disaggregation
Splitting a national statistic over a map, using a proxy that says where the quantity is likely to occur.


NUTS
The European classification of territorial units. NUTS 0 is the country level.



Eurostat reports NAI and removals by country, not by place. The routine therefore works in two stages. It first completes the national series, which is a statistical problem, and it then places the national values on a map, which is a spatial problem.






NoteWhere the data come from



The Eurostat tables are downloaded with the eurostat package, which reads the same data as the Eurostat website. The download script (scripts/03_download_eurostat.R) keeps only the volumes in thousand cubic metres, for the years 2000 to 2024.








NoteTwo reports are consulted for the method



INCA Part III (La Notte et al., 2021) defines the service and the NAI proxy, and INCA Part II (Vallecillo et al., 2019) (chapter 4) describes how national flows are spatialised. The Eurostat ecosystem accounts handbook (KS-01-26-019-EN-N) (Eurostat, 2026a) complements them. Its wood chapter treats FAWS as a cultivated context measured by net increment and forest not available for wood supply (FNAWS) as an uncultivated context measured by removals. None of the references gives a formula for timber overuse, so the check below defines overuse as removals greater than NAI.








NotePaths are relative to the project root



_quarto.yml sets execute-dir: project, so every path below resolves from the repository root regardless of where the .qmd file sits. There is no need for here::here() or setwd().

title: Wood Provision Ecosystem Service
text:
The spatial key
The spatial key follows the method of the INCA tool and of INCA Part II. Chapter 4 of INCA Part II spreads national flows over the forest classes of Corine Land Cover with dry matter productivity as a proxy (Vallecillo et al., 2019). The INCA wood provision tool does the same, multiplying a forest mask by an annual productivity layer and spreading each national value in proportion to the result. The Earth observation roadmap of the INCA project names the Gross Dry Matter Productivity (GDMP) of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service as the proxy for the provisioning services (Zurbarán Nucci et al., 2025). A decision was made to follow this method. Cells with more productive vegetation add more wood, so they receive a larger part of the national NAI.
The weight of a 100 m cell is 1 if it is forest in the Corine accounting layer of the year (broad-leaved, coniferous and mixed forest and transitional woodland and shrub, CLC 311, 312, 313 and 324) and 0 otherwise, times the annual productivity of the same year. The sources of productivity differ by year. The 1 km product, version 2, covers 2000, 2006 and 2012 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-a). The 300 m product, version 2, covers 2018 and 2024 (Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, n.d.-b). The weights only share a national value among the cells of a country, so a difference in level between the two products does not change any national total. The weight of a 1 km cell is the sum of the weights of the 100 cells of 100 m inside it.
Inside each country, the national NAI is spread in proportion to the weight of every cell. Cells without forest get no flow, and the cells of a country add up to its national value. The forest used for the weight is all forest and not only the forest available for wood supply. INCA Part II and the INCA tool do not restrict the spatial key to FAWS, because the thresholds that define availability are not common across countries and a map built on them can mislead (Vallecillo et al., 2019). The statistic that is spread is still the NAI of FAWS.
Three choices in this step deserve a short explanation. First, the maps use the projection EPSG:3035 (ETRS89 Lambert azimuthal equal-area), in which every cell covers the same area on the ground, so a share of a cell and a count of cells translate directly into areas. Second, the weights are built at 100 m and summed to 1 km, which keeps the files in the repository small. The maps at 100 m are kept outside the repository because of their size. Third, the sum of each country is conserved, which means that mapping redistributes the national NAI and neither adds nor removes any.

eu_countries <- vect(countries_file)
eu_countries <- eu_countries[eu_countries$eu27, ]
weights <- lapply(years_report, \(y) rast(file.path(weights_dir, sprintf("clc_gdmp_weight_1km_%s.tif", y))))
names(weights) <- years_report

title: Wood Provision Ecosystem Service
text:
Country grid and weights
Each 1 km cell is assigned to a country, and the weights of every country are added once per year.

country_ids <- make_country_ids(eu_countries, weights[[1]])
weight_sums <- lapply(weights, country_weight_sums, country_ids = country_ids)

title: Wood Provision Ecosystem Service
text:
Spreading the national NAI
For each reporting year, the helper spread_totals() multiplies every cell by its country factor (national NAI divided by the weight total of the country). The result is in thousand cubic metres per 1 km cell, and each year is saved as a compressed GeoTIFF in data/outputs/gis/.

for (yr in years_report) {
  flow_map <- spread_totals(
    totals = filter(nai_filled, year == yr),
    weight = weights[[as.character(yr)]],
    country_ids = country_ids,
    weight_sums = weight_sums[[as.character(yr)]]
  )
  names(flow_map) <- paste0("nai_clc_gdmp_", yr)
  writeRaster(
    flow_map,
    file.path(gis_dir, sprintf("wood_nai_clc_gdmp_1km_%s.tif", yr)),
    overwrite = TRUE,
    datatype = "FLT4S",
    gdal = c("COMPRESS=DEFLATE", "PREDICTOR=3", "TILED=YES")
  )
}

  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("nai_clc_gdmp_"), names_to = "year", values_to = "nai") |>
  mutate(year = sub("nai_clc_gdmp_", "", year)) |>
  filter(nai > 0)

ggplot(map_data) +
  geom_tile(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = nai)) +
  geom_sf(data = countries, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(transform = "sqrt", name = "1000 m3\nper 10 km cell") +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 3) +

title: Wood Provision Ecosystem Service
text:
Maps at 100 m
The maps at 100 m use the same key without the summation to 1 km, so a forest cell of 100 m receives its share of the national NAI. They are written by scripts/07_write_maps_100m.R, with the same conservation check, and they are too large for the repository. Each file weighs about 0.6 GB because continuous values compress poorly. They are delivered in an external folder together with a README that gives the grid, units, method and totals.
